notable: Opened in 1992 as one of the first retro-style ballparks and sparked a wave of neotraditional parks.
Replaced Memorial Stadium, the Orioles' home from 1954 until 1991.
The playing field sits 16 feet below street level.
Hosted the 1993 MLB All-Star Game.
The oldest active ballpark in Major League Baseball, opened April 20, 1912.
The left-field Green Monster wall stands about 37 feet tall.
Pesky's Pole in right field sits 302 feet from home plate.
Ted Williams's 1946 home run, measured at 502 feet, is the official longest at Fenway.
Hosted the 2009 and 2024 World Series, and the Yankees won the 2009 title there.
Its exterior and frieze copy the design of the original 1923 stadium next door.
Built with about 11,000 pieces of Indiana limestone.
New York City FC has used it as an interim home since 2015, until Etihad Park opens in 2027.

architect: HOK Sport, Lescher & Mahoney Sports, and Criswell, Blizzard & Blouin Architects
notable: The only nonretractable domed stadium in MLB, built on the former Gas Plant district site.
Hosted the first instant-replay use in MLB history, in September 2008.
Hurricane Milton destroyed much of the roof on October 9, 2024, and repairs finished in April 2026.
Has a cownose ray tank behind center field.
note: The Rays played the 2025 season at George M. Steinbrenner Field and returned to Tropicana Field on April 6, 2026. A planned roughly $2.3 billion stadium on the Hillsborough College Dale Mabry campus targets a 2029 opening but is not yet built. The city lease runs through 2027.

architect: Rod Robbie and Robbie Adjeleian (NORR Consortium); Populous (2024 renovation)
notable: The first major league stadium with a functional, fully retractable motorized roof.
An attached 348-room hotel, with 70 rooms overlooking the field.
Hosted games of both the 1992 and 1993 World Series, which the Blue Jays won.
Hosted games 1, 2, 6 and 7 of the 2025 World Series, which the Dodgers won.
Opened in 1991 as Comiskey Park, the first major sporting facility built in Chicago since 1929.
Hosted the 2005 World Series and the 2003 All-Star Game.
Mark Buehrle threw the franchise's first perfect game here in July 2009.
Renovations in 2001–2007 removed 6,600 upper-deck seats to address fan complaints.
note: Lease runs through the 2029 season. A proposed new ballpark at The 78 in the South Loop was under discussion; it was not approved in the latest source found.

notable: Its record attendance is 45,274, set in an October 1997 Division Series Game 5.
The team sold out 455 consecutive regular-season games between 1995 and 2001.
Hosted World Series games in 1995, 1997 and 2016, plus the 1997 All-Star Game.
Lit by 19 light towers that some have compared to oversized toothbrushes.

architect: Populous (then HOK Sport), with SHG and Rockwell Group
notable: Built in a retro-classic style, with an outfield fountain, a Ferris wheel and a carousel.
Hosted the 2005 All-Star Game and the 2006 and 2012 World Series.
Two no-hitters have been thrown here, both by Tigers pitchers, including Justin Verlander's in 2007.
The left-field video display, added for 2024, is MLB's second largest at 15,688 square feet.
note: Planned rename to Fifth Third Park before the 2027 season, after Fifth Third Bank acquired Comerica Bank.

notable: Opened April 10, 1973, with a 12–1 win over the Texas Rangers.
Nolan Ryan threw the first of his seven no-hitters here in 1973, three walks short of a perfect game.
Hosted the 1973 and 2012 All-Star Games and World Series games in 1980, 1985, 2014 and 2015.
The fountain behind right field is described as the largest privately funded fountain in the world.
note: In April 2026 the Royals and Hallmark Cards announced a new downtown ballpark at Crown Center, targeted to open for the 2030 season.

notable: Hosted the 2014 MLB All-Star Game.
ESPN The Magazine ranked it the top baseball stadium experience in North America in 2010.
Recertified LEED Gold in 2017, the first sports site in the nation to earn that level.
A center-field sign called Minnie and Paul lights up after home runs and Twins wins.
Opened in 2000 as Raley Field and kept that name until 2019.
The Sacramento River Cats play here too, and the two clubs alternate home dates when one is away.
The Athletics have a tenancy through 2027, with a Las Vegas ballpark targeted to open in 2028.
note: Capacity includes lawn and standing room; fixed seats total 10,624. Temporary home at Sutter Health Park for the 2025–2027 seasons; planned move to a 33,000-seat retractable-roof ballpark on the former Tropicana Las Vegas site, targeted for 2028.

architect: HOK Sport (now Populous) and Molina & Associates
notable: The roof usually opens only in April and May; most home games from 2000 to 2019 were played with it closed.
The Crawford Boxes sit 315 feet from home plate behind a 19-foot wall in left field.
Hosted World Series games in 2005, 2017, 2019, 2021 and 2022, and the 2022 clincher was played here.
Mike Fiers threw the ballpark's first no-hitter on August 21, 2015.

architect: Noble W. Herzberg and Associates (1966); HOK Sport, Robert A. M. Stern and Walt Disney Imagineering (renovation)
notable: Nicknamed The Big A, it is the fourth-oldest active ballpark in Major League Baseball.
Hosted the 2002 World Series and All-Star Games in 1967, 1989 and 2010.
Holds the record baseball crowd of 64,406 for an ALCS game on October 5, 1982.
The Angels extended their lease through 2032 in February 2025, and no relocation is planned.

surface: Kentucky bluegrass with overseeded perennial ryegrass
notable: A retractable roof covering about nine acres rides on 128 wheels and is usually left open.
The 'Pen is a standing-room area beside the bullpens where fans watch relievers warm up.
Hosted the All-Star Game in 2001 and 2023, and WrestleMania XIX drew a record 54,097 fans.
Opened in July 1999 as Safeco Field, and the Mariners have played here ever since.

surface: Synthetic grass (infield and warning track are clay)
notable: Hosted all six games of the 2020 World Series, the first such venue without its tenant in the Series.
Hosted Games 1 and 2 of the 2023 World Series, which the Rangers won in five games.
Hosted the 2024 MLB All-Star Game.
Globe Life holds the naming rights through 2048.

surface: Hybrid Bermuda overseeded with perennial ryegrass
notable: Opened in 2017 as SunTrust Park and was renamed in 2020 after the bank merger.
A metal canopy of about 108,000 square feet covers roughly 60 percent of the seats.
The ballpark sits alongside The Battery Atlanta mixed-use development.
The grass was changed to a hybrid Bermuda overseed with ryegrass before the 2023 season.

previous_stadium: Hard Rock Stadium, under earlier names Joe Robbie Stadium and Dolphin Stadium (1993–2011)
notable: Opened in 2012 as Marlins Park and was renamed after a 2021 naming-rights deal.
A retractable roof covers the field.
The grass field was replaced with Shaw Sports B1K artificial turf beginning in 2020.
Outfield walls were lowered during a 2016 renovation.
Opened in 2009 next to the site where Shea Stadium once stood.
The Jackie Robinson Rotunda entrance recalls Ebbets Field in Brooklyn.
The Home Run Apple rises beyond center field after Mets home runs.
Hosted the 2013 All-Star Game and three games of the 2015 World Series.
Opened April 3, 2004 in the South Philadelphia Sports Complex.
Monty's Angle, the left-center area, has distances of about 381 to 409 feet.
The left-field wall was moved back 5 feet after the 2005 season.
The stadium cost $458 million to build, about $781 million in 2025 dollars.

architect: HOK Sport and Devrouax & Purnell Architects and Planners
notable: Opened March 22, 2008 on the Anacostia River in D.C.'s Navy Yard neighborhood.
The stadium was not designed for a roof, and a 2013 proposal to add one was rejected.
Total cost reached $783.9 million once transportation, art and infrastructure work is included.
The Nationals left RFK Stadium after the 2007 season for this ballpark.
Oldest National League ballpark and second-oldest in MLB, behind only Fenway Park.
Ivy-covered brick outfield walls date to 1937 and were included in its 2004 landmark designation.
A hand-turned scoreboard in place since 1937 is one of the last of its kind in MLB.
It was the last MLB park to install lights, in 1988.

architect: HOK Sport (now Populous) and GBBN Architects
notable: Two smokestacks in right-center field spew flames and fireworks after Reds home runs and wins.
A gap in the seating lets fans see the downtown skyline from inside the park.
Hosted the 2015 MLB All-Star Game.
Adam Dunn hit an estimated 535-foot home run into the Ohio River in 2004, the park's longest.

architect: HKS, Inc.; NBBJ; Eppstein Uhen Architects
notable: Its fan-shaped retractable roof is the only one of its kind in North America.
Hosted the 2002 MLB All-Star Game, which ended in a tie.
Carlos Zambrano threw the park's first no-hitter during a 2008 Cubs-Astros series moved here by Hurricane Ike.
A July 1999 crane collapse killed three workers and delayed the opening.

architect: HOK Sport (now Populous) with L.D. Astorino & Associates
notable: Built on the North Shore beside the Allegheny River, with views of downtown Pittsburgh.
Its retro-classic design uses Kasota limestone and steel, echoing older parks like Forbes Field.
It had the first LED video boards in an outdoor MLB stadium.
Hosted the 2006 All-Star Game and the 2013 NL Wild Card Game, its first playoff contest.

architect: HOK Sport (now Populous) with Kennedy Associates
notable: Its 2006 debut season sold out every Cardinals game, drawing over 3.4 million fans.
The Cardinals won the 2006 and 2011 World Series titles at this ballpark.
Hosted the 2009 MLB All-Star Game.
The Gate 3 entrance has an arch that recalls the Eads Bridge.

surface: Shaw Sports Turf B1K synthetic turf
notable: Pioneered a retractable roof over natural grass before switching to artificial turf in 2019.
Arizona went 4-0 at home in the 2001 World Series, with games 1, 2, 6 and 7 played here.
Has a swimming pool in right-center field.
Hosted the 2011 All-Star Game and games 3 through 5 of the 2023 World Series.
Sits about 5,200 feet above sea level, the highest ballpark in the majors.
A humidor keeps the baseballs in check against the thin, dry air that favors hitters.
The center-field bleacher section is nicknamed the Rockpile.
Hideo Nomo threw the only no-hitter here through 2025, in 1996.
The oldest MLB ballpark west of the Mississippi River.
Holds more seats than any other baseball stadium in the world.
Has hosted the World Series twelve times and thirteen no-hitters, two of them perfect games.
Will host Olympic baseball again at the 2028 Summer Games.
note: Sources in 2026 list the venue as Uniqlo Field at Dodger Stadium, after a field naming-rights agreement.

architect: Populous (then HOK Sport) and Antoine Predock
notable: The historic Western Metal Supply Co. building was built into the park and forms the left-field foul pole.
Set a baseball attendance record of 47,773 against the Dodgers on October 9, 2024.
Hosted the 2006 World Baseball Classic final and the 2016 All-Star Game.
Naming rights went to a San Diego pet supplies retailer in 2004 for $60 million over 22 years.
The first MLB ballpark built without public money since Dodger Stadium in 1962.
Its right-field wall stands 24 feet high, the park's most distinctive feature.
The water beyond right field is informally called McCovey Cove.
Hosted games three through five of the 2002 World Series and the 2007 All-Star Game.
